title: A pool of fire and water
hook: in the world's pool we dwell, where water and fire both are, feet stuck in the mud of attachment (Asa M1, ang 12)
tomorrow: This human body is your chance

segments.voice: Yesterday, kartaa, the Maker, and your line, my master. Tonight's shabad is darker, and very honest.

Monsoon in a Punjabi village. The field path has turned to thick brown mud. You step off the bricks, and your foot sinks to the ankle. You pull. The mud pulls back. You pull harder, and your foot comes out, without the shoe. Mud like that has a rule: the harder you yank, the tighter it holds. Guru Nanak pictures the world as a pool with mud like that.
screen: `MONSOON. A FIELD PATH TURNED TO MUD.` → `THE HARDER YOU PULL, THE TIGHTER IT HOLDS.` → `GURU NANAK SAW THE WORLD LIKE THIS.`

segments.voice: The third So Purakh shabad is by Guru Nanak, in Raag Asa. It begins, in paraphrase: we live in that pool, and He made both water and fire there. A pool where water and fire live together: things that cool and things that burn, comfort and craving, side by side. Then the mud. In the mud of attachment, moh, the feet can't move. I have seen people drowning there. Moh is the clinging kind of love: to things, to status, to having it our way. It doesn't feel like a trap. It feels like the ground. Then the shabad turns to the mind: foolish mind, you don't remember the One. Forgetting the Lord, your virtues waste away. And then a turn. Guru Nanak doesn't present himself as the one standing safely on the bank. He says, in effect: I'm not a celibate ascetic, I'm not a model of virtue, I'm not learned. My life has been foolish and ignorant. Then the closing line: Nanak prays, I seek the shelter of those who have not forgotten You. So the way out of the mud isn't pulling harder on your own. It's reaching for a hand: the company of people who remember, the sangat. Not willpower alone, and not leaving the world behind. The shabad stays in the pool of fire and water, and reaches for those who remember. Out of the mud.
screen: `A POOL WHERE WATER AND FIRE LIVE.` · `MOH: THE MUD THAT HOLDS THE FEET.` · `NOT CELIBATE, NOT VIRTUOUS, NOT LEARNED.` · `SHELTER WITH THOSE WHO REMEMBER.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Lift your feet a little off the floor, wiggle your toes and feel how free they are, then set them down. Name one thing that's been holding your feet lately, a grudge, a habit, a worry you keep feeding, without yanking at it. Then think of one steady person who remembers, and picture taking their hand; if you pray, you can say Waheguru once.
Moh, attachment. Guru Nanak's picture of the world in Rehras: water and fire together, feet stuck in the mud of moh, and shelter with those who haven't forgotten the Lord.
Your line: out of the mud. Not by yanking harder, but by taking a hand. That's day four hundred eleven.

screen: `DAY 411 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THIS HUMAN BODY IS YOUR CHANCE.`

howItsDone: This shabad is the third of the So Purakh group in Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; Sikh teachers cite its closing line when explaining the place of sangat, the company of those who remember, in Sikh life.

pairs: the world: water and fire together

myth: in this shabad Guru Nanak presents himself as safely beyond the mud
he says he isn't celibate, virtuous or learned, and asks for shelter.
the shabad says the Lord made both water and fire in the pool
comfort and burning, side by side.
the way out, in this shabad, is to leave the world behind
it asks for the shelter of those who remember.

fork.setup: your feet are stuck in the mud of attachment. what does Guru Nanak do in the shabad?
options: says he isn't virtuous or learned, and seeks the shelter of those who remember.
fork.reveal: he admits he has no merit of his own and asks for shelter with those who have not forgotten the Lord: a hand, not a harder pull.

original.note: Gurmukhi: moh, attachment; in this shabad, the mud in which the feet cannot move.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pool of fire and water is a picture of hell.
what it means: it's this world, where comfort and burning live together and attachment holds the feet like mud.
what a scholar hears: the word read as mud here is pankaj, which elsewhere means the lotus, the flower born of mud; commentators take it as the mire of attachment in this line.
guess: attachment, the clinging that holds you
a deep hatred that pushes people away

chat.says: In that shabad Guru Nanak sees people stuck in mud. How does he say they get out?
options: By seeking the shelter of those who haven't forgotten the One: the sangat.
By first becoming learned and virtuous enough to climb out alone.
By pulling harder on their own until their willpower frees them.
chat.meaning: Guru Nanak calls himself not celibate, not virtuous, not learned, and prays for the shelter of those who have not forgotten the Lord.

moh.meaning: attachment, the clinging kind of love

sangat.meaning: the company of people who remember the One

Raag Asa.meaning: one of the musical modes the hymns are set in

So Purakh.meaning: that Being: the second group of Rehras shabads
